questions.q: What is the modulus of the complex number \( z = -5 + 12i \)? Write the formula and compute the exact value.
questions.a: The modulus is \( |z| = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13 \). A wrong answer like \( \sqrt{-25 + 144} = \sqrt{119} \) reveals the student is squaring the imaginary unit \( i \) instead of treating the coefficient 12 as a real number, confusing algebraic form with the modulus formula.

questions.q: If \( z = 2 - 3i \), what is \( z \cdot \bar{z} \)? How does this relate to \( |z|^2 \)? Explain why this relationship holds for any complex number.
questions.a: \( \bar{z} = 2 + 3i \), so \( z \cdot \bar{z} = (2 - 3i)(2 + 3i) = 4 - 9i^2 = 4 + 9 = 13 \). Also \( |z| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{13} \), so \( |z|^2 = 13 \). The identity \( z\bar{z} = |z|^2 \) holds because \( (a+ib)(a-ib) = a^2 - (ib)^2 = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2 \). A wrong answer like \( (2-3i)(2-3i) = 4 - 12i + 9i^2 = -5 -12i \) shows the student confused conjugate with the original number, missing the sign change in the imaginary part.

questions.q: Simplify \( \frac{3 + 4i}{1 - 2i} \) by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. Express your answer in standard form \( a + ib \).
questions.a: Multiply by \( \frac{1 + 2i}{1 + 2i} \): Numerator: \( (3+4i)(1+2i) = 3 + 6i + 4i + 8i^2 = 3 + 10i - 8 = -5 + 10i \). Denominator: \( (1-2i)(1+2i) = 1 - 4i^2 = 1 + 4 = 5 \). Result: \( \frac{-5 + 10i}{5} = -1 + 2i \). A wrong answer like \( -5 + 10i \) (forgetting to divide by 5) or \( \frac{-5 + 10i}{1 - 4i} \) (not simplifying denominator) reveals the student doesn't recognize that the conjugate product yields a real denominator, which is the entire purpose of this technique.

questions.q: Given \( z_1 = 1 + i \) and \( z_2 = 2 - i \), verify whether \( |z_1 z_2| = |z_1| |z_2| \) and \( \overline{z_1 z_2} = \bar{z_1} \bar{z_2} \). What do these properties tell you about the algebraic structure?
questions.a: \( z_1 z_2 = (1+i)(2-i) = 2 - i + 2i - i^2 = 3 + i \). \( |z_1 z_2| = \sqrt{3^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{10} \). \( |z_1| = \sqrt{2} \), \( |z_2| = \sqrt{5} \), product \( = \sqrt{10} \). Equal. \( \overline{z_1 z_2} = 3 - i \). \( \bar{z_1} = 1-i \), \( \bar{z_2} = 2+i \), product \( = (1-i)(2+i) = 2 + i - 2i - i^2 = 3 - i \). Equal. These show modulus is multiplicative and conjugation is an automorphism — both preserve the algebraic structure. A wrong answer where the student computes \( |z_1 z_2| \) as \( |z_1| + |z_2| \) reveals additive thinking instead of multiplicative, a common error when generalizing from real absolute value properties.

questions.q: A student claims: "For any complex number \( z \), \( |z^2| = |z|^2 \) and \( \overline{z^2} = (\bar{z})^2 \)." Is this always true? Justify your answer with a proof or counterexample.
questions.a: Yes, always true. Proof: \( |z^2| = |z \cdot z| = |z| \cdot |z| = |z|^2 \) (using multiplicativity of modulus). \( \overline{z^2} = \overline{z \cdot z} = \bar{z} \cdot \bar{z} = (\bar{z})^2 \) (using conjugation distributes over multiplication). These are special cases of the general properties \( |z_1 z_2| = |z_1||z_2| \) and \( \overline{z_1 z_2} = \bar{z_1}\bar{z_2} \). A wrong answer claiming it's false with a counterexample like \( z = 1+i \) (where \( z^2 = 2i \), \( |z^2| = 2 \), \( |z|^2 = (\sqrt{2})^2 = 2 \) — actually equal!) reveals the student made an arithmetic error in computing powers or moduli, not a conceptual flaw.

questions.q: Create a complex number \( z \) such that \( |z| = 5 \) and \( \text{Re}(z) = 3 \). How many such numbers exist? Find all of them and plot them on the Argand plane.
questions.a: Let \( z = 3 + iy \). Then \( |z| = \sqrt{3^2 + y^2} = 5 \Rightarrow 9 + y^2 = 25 \Rightarrow y^2 = 16 \Rightarrow y = \pm 4 \). Two numbers: \( 3 + 4i \) and \( 3 - 4i \). They are symmetric about the real axis (conjugates). A poor answer giving only \( 3 + 4i \) misses the negative root, revealing the student forgets that modulus uses \( y^2 \), losing sign information — a key insight that conjugate pairs share the same modulus.
